newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD grapples with globalising trade, jobs, bribes.
newsitem.headline: OECD grapples with globalising trade, jobs, bribes.

text.p: Ministers from the 29 countries of the OECD on Monday began a two-day annual summit to debate the economic benefits and social drawbacks of increasingly global trade and to compare notes on fighting unemployment.

The talks will also focus on the fight against corruption and criminalising bribery of state officials in business transactions, after the announcement by U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley on Friday night that agreement had been reached on how member countries should start legislating against it.

The ministers are also set to offer a "friendly-but-firm" signal on a Russian membership request, with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov arriving on Tuesday to sign an agreement on closer ties with the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development.

The OECD's Canadian Secretary General, Donald Johnston, told reporters ahead of the summit that Russian membership was a long term goal but that Moscow still had a long way to go on reform before starting talks on joining the free-market organisation.

On bribery, where the United States has been at loggerheads with France and Germany, Daley told reporters in Washington on Friday a deal had been reached in which OECD states agreed to introduce laws by April 1998 criminalising bribery of foreign state officials in business dealings and simultaneously start talks on a treaty which would achieve the same end.

France, whose finance minister Jean Arthuis is chairing the meeting, had lined up with Germany to push for a fully fledged treaty which would harmonise anti-bribery legislation instead of leaving it up to each country to decide how to go about it.

On the economic front, the meeting, which is being attended by a mix of ministers for finance, trade, social and foreign affairs, is set to devote most of day one to globalisation, as increasing international trade pitches countries as well as companies into competition for business and investment.

Highlighting the policy dilemmas involved at an organisation whose main goal is promoting a more "liberal" economic strategy is a report which shows structural unemployment has risen during the 1990s but which commends those who have reformed along the lines espoused by the OECD.

The report prepared for the meeting praises Ireland and the Netherlands for reducing structural unemployment, by cutting unemployment benefit and raising education levels in the first case and wage moderation and payroll tax cuts in the latter.
The report says overall unemployment among 23 of the 29 member countries -- the most recent members are not included -- rose to 7.7 percent in 1996 from 6.1 percent in 1990.

Structural unemployment, which strips out the portion of joblessness attributed to the ups and downs of the economic cycle, stood at 7.1 percent in 1996, versus 6.8 percent at the start of the decade, the report says.

It says other countries like France and Germany have had greater difficulty reforming labour markets and -- though it recognises the value of policies which strive to reduce social inequality -- suggests they too should change their unemployment benefit systems and make their labour markets more flexible.
